prompt: An architect who last opened the repository a year ago reviews a design and calls it "a two-week job". The team says two months. By lesson 15, what is the likeliest explanation?

choices.text: The team is protecting itself with a long estimate
choices.why: Possible, but the lesson's first suspect is the reading of somebody away from the code for a year.

choices.text: His sense of the cost drifted
choices.why: Right: experience decays when it stops being renewed, and drift is felt by nobody.

choices.text: The design is wrong and should be rejected
choices.why: Nothing says the design is wrong; it may only be mispriced.

choices.text: Two months is the time a review takes
choices.why: The estimate is for building, not for reviewing.

prompt: Alistair Cockburn's name for a tiny version of the system that runs one small function end to end, through every main part, is the ___ skeleton.
hint: Lesson 15, the figure with one line through every box.

prompt: Match each author to the idea the course takes from them.

pairs.right: Architectus oryzus, who mentors rather than decides alone
the architect riding between penthouse and engine room

prompt: Which of these suit an architect's two half-days a week, by lesson 15? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A fitness function for a rule the architect set
choices.why: Yes: off every critical path by construction, and it keeps working in meetings.

choices.text: The last story before a release
choices.why: The release would wait on an interrupted calendar.

choices.text: A slow query from a team's backlog, chosen with that team
choices.why: Yes: a small fix in the real code, which nobody is waiting for.

choices.text: A three-day spike on a library's behaviour under load
choices.why: Yes: a question the architect has asked, answered inside a time box.

choices.text: Sole ownership of the migration's core module
choices.why: That is the critical path again; pairing with the owner is the alternative.

prompt: A team waves the architect's pull requests through without comments. By lesson 15, what is lost?

choices.text: Nothing, since the architect's code is reviewed by the architect
choices.why: Self-review is not the team's review, and the lesson asks for the team's.

choices.text: Speed, because reviews slow the architect down
choices.why: The architect's code is off the critical path, so review costs no release anything.

choices.text: The review, and the message that conventions bind her too
choices.why: Right: a team that does not review her is not reviewing, and the juniors learn rank instead.

choices.text: Her authority, since unreviewed code looks careless
choices.why: The loss is to the team's habits, more than to how she looks.

prompt: An architect can no longer run the company's system on a laptop from a clean checkout. By lesson 15, what is the cheapest response?
hint: Lesson 15: most of the five questions have the same answer.

choices.text: Ask Platform for a hosted environment to use instead
choices.why: That works around the symptom and leaves her outside the code the team runs.

choices.text: Change something small in the code this week
choices.why: Right: getting the setup running again is the first step of that change, and it recalibrates.

choices.text: Accept it as a normal part of seniority
choices.why: The lesson accepts coding less, never stopping; this is a sign of drift.
Reading tells her how it was meant to work; changing something tells her how it works now.
